doc.title: Pete Barbutti interviewed by Monk Rowe, via Zoom, December 8, 2022

title: Shy kid, accordion lessons and high school band
summary: Painfully shy as a child, accordion gave him confidence; studied with Professor Sebastianelli, then high school band with Gene Morris and Charlie Coleman.

story.theme_name: Growing up and learning music: family, first instruments, teachers
story.community_name: School days: grades, teachers and leaving school

blocks.x: What were you like as a junior high student?

Well first of all let me back up a little, I was incredibly shy as a kid. I mean unbelievably. In fact I just remembered the other day when I needed new shoes I was too shy to even go in the shoe store so my sister, who was like eight years older, she would go in the store and bring the shoes out and try them on me in the car. I mean it was almost like an emotional thing. And I was like that until at age nine or ten they said, “You should take accordion lessons.” ‘Cause everybody in the neighborhood, all the Italian kids played the accordion, all the Jewish kids played violin, and the girls played piano. Piano was considered feminine. Strangely enough I went to see Arturo Sandoval at his invitation which I was thrilled with because I love him. And he said the same thing in the Cuban culture, the piano is considered feminine, so he used to practice the piano but he had to hide it because people would think he was gay if he played the piano you know. But everybody, my cousin and I, my cousin Ray and I got, we both took accordion lessons and we both had a beginner-style accordion and I studied with Professor Sebastianelli and of course the first four or five months was nothing but solfeggio, you know just singing the notes without playing the accordion. Then when I’d get home I’d play the accordion. And that sort of gave me a reason to be different on stage or to go out in public, it sort of gave me some confidence. And then when I got into high school, we had a hot shot baseball team, we won the city championship and so I was more into sports and running track. And I had to take an elective subject so I said well I’ll take band. And the professor, the teacher there was a guy named Gene Morris. He was in a Navy band, played trombone, he was a very hip guy, and he was a great arranger and everything. I mean he was — and very today. And there was a piano player who was in the band too, his name was Charlie Coleman. And Charlie was way above his pay grade. Charlie was — I mean we used to go down to the record store and play a Stan Kenton record, you know. In the old days you went in the booth and while you were there you could play the record. He’d play it four or five times and then he’d go home and he could score it for the band. I mean in high school. So Charlie was a year older than me, graduated a year before I did. And I wasn’t sure what I was going to do but I loved music so very much and having the accordion was — it changed everything.
